title: Ἑκατόμβη
titleEn: The Hecatomb and Thetis’ Plea — Iliad 1.413–510
about: Thetis answers Achilles. She laments that she bore him to so short and sorrowful a life, promises to take his request to Zeus on Olympus when the gods return from a twelve-day feast among the Ethiopians, and tells him to sit by the ships, keep his wrath and stay out of the war. She leaves him angry for the girl who was taken from him. Meanwhile Odysseus brings Chryseis to Chryse. The crew furl the sail, moor the ship and land the hecatomb, and Odysseus puts the girl in her father’s hands. Chryses prays to Apollo, who made the Achaeans suffer for his sake once before, to turn the plague from the Danaans, and the god hears him. They sacrifice, feast and sing a paean all day, and next morning sail back to the Achaean camp on a wind that Apollo sends, and beach the ship. Achilles sits angry by his ships and does not fight. On the twelfth dawn the gods go back to Olympus, and Thetis rises from the sea, finds Zeus sitting apart, takes his knees and his chin, and asks him to honour her son by giving the Trojans strength until the Achaeans pay him honour.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Θέτις κατὰ δάκρυ χέουσα·
sentences.l: Him then answered Thetis, down a tear shedding:
sentences.i: Then Thetis answered him, shedding tears:
sentences.n: Achilles’ speech ended at 412, and this line brings in his mother’s reply; it is the answering formula the poem used for Agamemnon at 172, with Thetis as the speaker. τὸν is ‘him’ (the article as a pronoun), and ἠμείβετ’ is ἠμείβετο ‘answered’, elided. κατὰ δάκρυ χέουσα is ‘shedding a tear’: δάκρυ is ‘tear’, χέουσα the participle of χέω ‘pour’, and κατά stands apart from it (tmesis), so the tears are poured down. Thetis is the mother who rose from the grey sea at 359.

sentences.t: ὤ μοι τέκνον ἐμόν, τί νύ σ’ ἔτρεφον αἰνὰ τεκοῦσα;
sentences.l: “Ah me, my child, why then did I rear you, dreadfully having borne you?
sentences.i: “Ah me, my child, why did I rear you, when I had borne you in such dread?
sentences.n: ὤ μοι is ‘ah me’, and τέκνον ἐμόν ‘my child’ (τέκνον is ‘child’, the word she used to him at 362). The question has two verbs: ἔτρεφον, imperfect of τρέφω ‘rear’, and τεκοῦσα, aorist participle of τίκτω ‘bear’, which is earlier than the main verb, ‘having borne’. αἰνά is the neuter plural of αἰνός ‘dread’ used as an adverb. The Greek does not say whose dread it is, her pains in giving birth or the fate he was born to, and the English leaves this open. νύ is a particle that sharpens the question. The edition ends it with the Greek question mark.

sentences.t:
αἴθ’ ὄφελες παρὰ νηυσὶν ἀδάκρυτος καὶ ἀπήμων
ἧσθαι, ἐπεί νύ τοι αἶσα μίνυνθά περ οὔ τι μάλα δήν·
sentences.l:
Would that you ought, by the ships, tearless and unharmed,
to sit, since now for you the portion is for a little while, not very long at all;
sentences.i: If only you were sitting by the ships without tears and unharmed, since your lot lasts only a little while, not long at all;
sentences.n: αἴθ’ ὄφελες with an infinitive is a wish that cannot now come true: literally ‘would that you ought to sit’, that is, ‘if only you were sitting’. ὄφελες belongs to the verb ὀφείλω ‘owe, ought’. ἀδάκρυτος is ‘tearless’ (ἀ- ‘not’ + δάκρυ ‘tear’) and ἀπήμων ‘unharmed’ (ἀ- + πῆμα ‘woe’); ἧσθαι is the infinitive of ἥμαι ‘sit’. αἶσα, ‘portion’, is the share of life allotted to a man, and μίνυνθα ‘for a little while’ is repeated and sharpened by οὔ τι μάλα δήν ‘not at all very long’; περ adds force to the first.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἅμα τ’ ὠκύμορος καὶ ὀϊζυρὸς περὶ πάντων
ἔπλεο· τώ σε κακῇ αἴσῃ τέκον ἐν μεγάροισι.
sentences.l:
but now at once swift-doomed and sorrowful beyond all
you have come to be; therefore under an evil portion I bore you in the halls.
sentences.i: But now you have come to be, beyond all others, both swift to your doom and a man of sorrow; that is why I bore you in the halls under an evil lot.
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ sets what is against what she wished. ὠκύμορος is ‘swift-doomed’ (ὠκύς ‘swift’ + μόρος ‘doom’), and ὀϊζυρός ‘sorrowful’; ἅμα τε … καὶ puts them together, ‘at once … and’, and περὶ πάντων ‘beyond all’ lifts him above everyone else. ἔπλεο is the second person of πέλομαι ‘be, become’, ‘you have come to be’. τώ is ‘therefore’. κακῇ αἴσῃ is a dative of attendant circumstance, ‘under an evil portion’, the same αἶσα as in 416; τέκον is an unaugmented aorist (compare τεκοῦσα in 414); μεγάροισι is the dative plural of μέγαρον ‘hall’. At 505 she uses ὠκύμορος again in the superlative.

sentences.t:
τοῦτο δέ τοι ἐρέουσα ἔπος Διὶ τερπικεραύνῳ
εἶμ’ αὐτὴ πρὸς Ὄλυμπον ἀγάννιφον αἴ κε πίθηται.
sentences.l:
And this word, to say it for you to Zeus delighting-in-the-thunderbolt,
I will go myself to very snowy Olympus, if he may be persuaded.
sentences.i: To say this word for you to Zeus, who delights in the thunderbolt, I will go myself to snowy Olympus, in case he can be persuaded.
sentences.n: She promises to carry the request herself. ἐρέουσα is the future participle of ἐρέω ‘I will say’, ‘intending to say’, and gives the purpose of the journey; τοι is σοι ‘for you’. Διὶ τερπικεραύνῳ is Zeus with a stock epithet, translated every time: τέρπω ‘delight’ + κεραυνός ‘thunderbolt’, ‘delighting in the thunderbolt’. εἶμι is a present form with the sense of the future, ‘I will go’. ἀγάννιφον is ‘very snowy’ (ἀγα- strengthens, as in ἀγακλυτός, and νίφω is ‘snow’); the formation is not quite certain. αἴ κε πίθηται is ‘if he may be persuaded’, aorist subjunctive middle of πείθω.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν νῦν νηυσὶ παρήμενος ὠκυπόροισι
μήνι’ Ἀχαιοῖσιν, πολέμου δ’ ἀποπαύεο πάμπαν·
sentences.l:
But you for now, by the swift-faring ships sitting,
be wrathful against the Achaeans, and from war cease altogether;
sentences.i: But for now sit by your swift-faring ships, be wrathful against the Achaeans, and cease from war altogether;
sentences.n: Thetis tells him what to do while she is gone: stay out of the fighting and keep his anger. μήνι’ is the imperative of μηνίω ‘be wrathful’, the verb of μῆνις ‘wrath’, and takes the dative Ἀχαιοῖσιν ‘against the Achaeans’. παρήμενος is ‘sitting beside’, which is how he is found again at 488. ἀποπαύεο is the middle imperative of ἀποπαύω ‘stop’, with the genitive πολέμου ‘from war’, and πάμπαν is ‘altogether’. ὠκυπόροισι ‘swift-faring’ (ὠκύς ‘swift’ + πόρος ‘passage’) is the stock epithet of ships. The σὺ μὲν νῦν of this line is answered by the δέ of 425, which sets what will happen on the twelfth day against what he must do now.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς γὰρ ἐς Ὠκεανὸν μετ’ ἀμύμονας Αἰθιοπῆας
χθιζὸς ἔβη κατὰ δαῖτα, θεοὶ δ’ ἅμα πάντες ἕποντο·
sentences.l:
for Zeus to Oceanus, among the blameless Ethiopians,
yesterday went for the feast, and the gods together all followed;
sentences.i: For Zeus went yesterday to Oceanus, among the blameless Ethiopians, for a feast, and all the gods went with him;
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason she cannot go to Zeus at once: he is away. Ὠκεανόν is Oceanus, named here as a place that Zeus can travel to, and Αἰθιοπῆας is the epic accusative plural of Αἰθίοψ (Attic Αἰθίοπας), the Ethiopians. ἀμύμονας ‘blameless’ is their epithet and is translated here though nothing in the line earns it. χθιζός is an adjective used like an adverb, ‘yesterday’; κατὰ δαῖτα is ‘for the feast’; ἕποντο is the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’, so all the gods went along with him.

sentences.t:
δωδεκάτῃ δέ τοι αὖτις ἐλεύσεται Οὔλυμπον δέ,
καὶ τότ’ ἔπειτά τοι εἶμι Διὸς ποτὶ χαλκοβατὲς δῶ,
καί μιν γουνάσομαι καί μιν πείσεσθαι ὀΐω.
sentences.l:
And on the twelfth, for you, again he will come to Olympus,
and then thereupon for you I will go to the bronze-floored house of Zeus,
and I will entreat him, and him to be persuaded I think.”
sentences.i: On the twelfth day he will come back to Olympus, and then I will go for you to the house of Zeus with the bronze floor, and entreat him, and I think he will be persuaded.”
sentences.n: δωδεκάτῃ is ‘on the twelfth’, with the word for ‘day’ left unsaid; line 493 picks up the count. Οὔλυμπον δέ is ‘to Olympus’ (-δε marks the goal), and the edition prints the name sometimes Ὄλυμπον (420) and sometimes Οὔλυμπον, two spellings of one word. χαλκοβατὲς δῶ is ‘the bronze-floored house’: δῶ is short for δῶμα, and whether βατός means ‘floor’ or ‘threshold’ is disputed. γουνάσομαι is the future of γουνάζομαι ‘entreat’, formed from γόνυ ‘knee’, because the suppliant clasps the knees (as she does at 500). πείσεσθαι is the future infinitive of πείθω, ‘will be persuaded’, with ὀΐω ‘I think’. Her speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασ’ ἀπεβήσετο, τὸν δὲ λίπ’ αὐτοῦ
χωόμενον κατὰ θυμὸν ἐϋζώνοιο γυναικὸς
τήν ῥα βίῃ ἀέκοντος ἀπηύρων·
sentences.i: With those words she went away and left him there, incensed at heart for the well-girdled woman whom they had taken from him by force, unwilling as he was;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασ’ is the usual close of a speech, ‘so then, having spoken’. ἀπεβήσετο is an aorist in -σετο (compare ἀνεδύσετο at 496), ‘went away’, and αὐτοῦ is ‘there, on the spot’. χωόμενον … γυναικός: χώομαι is ‘be incensed’, and the genitive says over what, ‘for the woman’. ἐϋζώνοιο ‘well-girdled’ (ἐΰ ‘well’ + ζώνη ‘girdle’) is her stock epithet. ἀπηύρων is ‘they took away’ (ἀπαυράω), and the ‘they’ are the heralds of 320 and following; ἀέκοντος, ‘of him unwilling’, is the genitive of the man robbed, with no pronoun written.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἐς Χρύσην ἵκανεν ἄγων ἱερὴν ἑκατόμβην.
sentences.l:
but Odysseus
to Chryse came, leading the sacred hecatomb.
sentences.i: But Odysseus reached Chryse, leading the sacred hecatomb.
sentences.n: The scene changes from Achilles to the ship that sailed at 312 carrying Chryseis. The second half of 430 begins the new sentence. Χρύσην is the place Chryse, the town of the priest Chryses (the man is Χρύσης), which his prayer named at 37. ἵκανεν is the imperfect of ἱκάνω ‘come to’, and ἄγων ‘leading’ goes with ἱερὴν ἑκατόμβην ‘the sacred hecatomb’, the offering Calchas said must be taken to Chryse along with her (99), a great sacrifice that need not be a hundred beasts.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ λιμένος πολυβενθέος ἐντὸς ἵκοντο
ἱστία μὲν στείλαντο, θέσαν δ’ ἐν νηῒ μελαίνῃ,
ἱστὸν δ’ ἱστοδόκῃ πέλασαν προτόνοισιν ὑφέντες
καρπαλίμως, τὴν δ’ εἰς ὅρμον προέρεσσαν ἐρετμοῖς.
sentences.l:
And they, when indeed within the very deep harbour they had come,
the sails they furled, and placed them in the black ship,
and the mast to the mast-holder they brought, lowering it with the forestays
swiftly, and her into the anchorage they rowed forward with oars.
sentences.i: When they had come inside the deep harbour, they furled the sails and laid them in the black ship; they lowered the mast with the forestays, swiftly, and brought it to its holder, and rowed the ship forward with oars into the anchorage.
sentences.n: The ship comes into harbour, and the sailors’ jobs are named in the order they are done. The first line is also in the Odyssey, with its English kept (πολυβενθέος ‘very deep’). The main verbs begin in the second: ἱστία … στείλαντο ‘they furled the sails’ (middle of στέλλω) and θέσαν ‘they placed’, an unaugmented aorist of τίθημι. ἱστοδόκῃ is the mast-holder, the rest on which the lowered mast lies, and goes with πέλασαν ‘brought near’; ὑφέντες ‘lowering’ goes with προτόνοισιν ‘with the forestays’. τὴν is the ship, εἰς ὅρμον ‘into the anchorage’, προέρεσσαν ‘rowed forward’ and ἐρετμοῖς ‘with oars’.

sentences.t: ἐκ δ’ εὐνὰς ἔβαλον, κατὰ δὲ πρυμνήσι’ ἔδησαν·
sentences.l: and out they threw the anchor-stones, and down they bound the stern-cables;
sentences.i: they cast out the anchor-stones and made fast the stern-cables;
sentences.n: The ship is moored for the night: εὐνάς, literally ‘beds’, are the anchor-stones thrown out from the bow, and πρυμνήσι’ are the cables from the stern, made fast to the shore. The line is word for word in the Odyssey, and its English is kept. ἐκ … ἔβαλον ‘threw out’ and κατὰ … ἔδησαν ‘bound down’ each have the preverb standing apart from the verb (tmesis).

sentences.t:
ἐκ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ βαῖνον ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης,
ἐκ δ’ ἑκατόμβην βῆσαν ἑκηβόλῳ Ἀπόλλωνι·
sentences.l:
and out also themselves they stepped upon the surf-line of the sea,
and out the hecatomb they made go, for far-shooting Apollo;
sentences.i: and they themselves stepped out onto the shore where the sea breaks, and led the hecatomb out for far-shooting Apollo;
sentences.n: The landing goes in order, the crew and then the beasts, and each clause begins with ἐκ ‘out’. βαῖνον is the imperfect of βαίνω ‘step’, but βῆσαν, from the same verb, is transitive, ‘made go’, so the hecatomb is led ashore. The first line is also in the Odyssey, and its English is kept (ῥηγμῖνι, ‘the surf-line’, is the place where the waves break). ἑκηβόλῳ ‘far-shooting’ is the epithet of Apollo, from ἑκάς ‘far’ and βάλλω ‘throw, shoot’, the usual explanation.

sentences.t: ἐκ δὲ Χρυσηῒς νηὸς βῆ ποντοπόροιο.
sentences.l: and out of the sea-crossing ship Chryseis stepped.
sentences.i: and Chryseis stepped out of the sea-crossing ship.
sentences.n: The girl is named last, because it is for her that everything has been done. Χρυσηΐς is built from Χρύσης, ‘daughter of Chryses’, in the same way as Βρισηΐς from Βρισεύς. βῆ is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω ‘went, stepped’. ἐκ stands first and its noun νηός ‘ship’ comes after Χρυσηΐς and before the verb, while the epithet ποντοπόροιο ‘sea-crossing’ (πόντος ‘sea’ + πόρος ‘passage’) is held back until after it; the Odyssey uses the epithet of ships.

sentences.t:
τὴν μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἐπὶ βωμὸν ἄγων πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεὺς
πατρὶ φίλῳ ἐν χερσὶ τίθει καί μιν προσέειπεν·
sentences.l:
Her then to the altar leading, many-wiled Odysseus
to her dear father in his hands placed, and addressed him:
sentences.i: Then Odysseus of many wiles led her to the altar, placed her in her dear father’s hands, and said to him:
sentences.n: Odysseus hands the girl back before he speaks. τὴν μέν is Chryseis, ‘her’, and ἐπὶ βωμόν ‘to the altar’ (βωμός, with a sacrifice in view) is where Chryses stands. πολύμητις ‘many-wiled’ is Odysseus’ stock epithet (μῆτις is cunning intelligence). τίθει is the imperfect of τίθημι ‘was placing’, and πατρὶ φίλῳ ‘to her dear father’ is Chryses, who is named in the next line. μιν is ‘him’, the father, and προσέειπεν ‘addressed’ opens the speech.

sentences.t:
ὦ Χρύση, πρό μ’ ἔπεμψεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων
παῖδά τε σοὶ ἀγέμεν, Φοίβῳ θ’ ἱερὴν ἑκατόμβην
ῥέξαι ὑπὲρ Δαναῶν ὄφρ’ ἱλασόμεσθα ἄνακτα,
ὃς νῦν Ἀργείοισι πολύστονα κήδε’ ἐφῆκεν.
sentences.l:
“O Chryses, forth me sent the lord of men, Agamemnon
the child to you to lead, and to Phoebus a sacred hecatomb
to offer on behalf of the Danaans, so that we may appease the lord,
who now upon the Argives much-groaning sorrows has sent.”
sentences.i: “Chryses, Agamemnon, lord of men, has sent me forth to bring you your child, and to offer a sacred hecatomb to Phoebus on behalf of the Danaans, so that we may appease the lord who has now sent upon the Argives sorrows that bring many a groan.”
sentences.n: Odysseus names what he brings and why. ὦ Χρύση is the vocative, and πρό … ἔπεμψεν ‘sent forth’ has its preverb apart (tmesis). ἀγέμεν is the infinitive of ἄγω in the Homeric ending -έμεν (Attic -ειν), and with ῥέξαι (aorist infinitive of ῥέζω ‘do, offer’) it gives the purpose of the sending. ὄφρ’ ἱλασόμεσθα is ‘so that we may appease’ (ἱλάσκομαι), a form in -ο- that does the work of a subjunctive. ἄνακτα, ‘the lord’, is Apollo. Δαναῶν and Ἀργείοισι are two names of the army. πολύστονα is ‘much-groaning’ (πολύς + στόνος ‘groan’), said of the κήδεα ‘sorrows’, and ἐφῆκεν ‘sent upon’ is the aorist of ἐφίημι.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ἐν χερσὶ τίθει, ὃ δὲ δέξατο χαίρων
παῖδα φίλην·
sentences.l:
So having spoken, in his hands he placed her, and he received her, rejoicing,
his dear child;
sentences.i: With these words he placed her in her father’s hands, and he took his dear child, rejoicing;
sentences.n: The handing over is told in two verbs, one for each man: τίθει ‘was placing’ is Odysseus, as at 441, and δέξατο ‘received’ is Chryses, ὃ δέ ‘and he’ (the article as a pronoun). ὣς εἰπών is ‘so having spoken’, the close of Odysseus’ speech, and χαίρων ‘rejoicing’ is what the old man is while he takes her. παῖδα φίλην, ‘his dear child’, is held to the start of the next line.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ὦκα θεῷ ἱερὴν ἑκατόμβην
ἑξείης ἔστησαν ἐΰδμητον περὶ βωμόν,
χερνίψαντο δ’ ἔπειτα καὶ οὐλοχύτας ἀνέλοντο.
sentences.l:
and they quickly for the god the sacred hecatomb
in order set up around the well-built altar,
and washed their hands then and took up the barley-for-sprinkling.
sentences.i: and they quickly set the sacred hecatomb in order around the well-built altar for the god, then washed their hands and took up the barley for sprinkling.
sentences.n: The rite begins, and τοί ‘they’ shifts the subject from Odysseus to the crew. ἔστησαν is the transitive aorist ‘set up, made stand’, ἑξείης ‘in order’, and ἐΰδμητον ‘well-built’ (ἐΰ ‘well’ + δέμω ‘build’) is the altar’s epithet. χερνίψαντο, from χέρνιψ ‘water for the hands’, is ‘washed their hands’, the cleansing before sacrifice. οὐλοχύτας are the grains of barley that are thrown on the victim, as in the Odyssey’s sacrifices, and ἀνέλοντο is ‘took up’.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δὲ Χρύσης μεγάλ’ εὔχετο χεῖρας ἀνασχών·
sentences.l: And for them Chryses loudly prayed, his hands raising:
sentences.i: And Chryses prayed loudly for them, raising his hands:
sentences.n: The posture of prayer is given in the participle χεῖρας ἀνασχών ‘raising his hands’. τοῖσιν ‘for them’ is a dative of interest, since Chryses prays on behalf of the Achaeans. μεγάλα, the neuter plural of μέγας used as an adverb, is ‘loudly’; εὔχετο is the imperfect of εὔχομαι ‘pray’. The prayer that follows opens with the same two lines as his first prayer at 37–38, so that the reader hears the first request again and then a different one.

sentences.t:
κλῦθί μευ ἀργυρότοξ’, ὃς Χρύσην ἀμφιβέβηκας
Κίλλαν τε ζαθέην Τενέδοιό τε ἶφι ἀνάσσεις·
sentences.l:
“Hear me, silver-bowed one, who stand-over Chryse
and Cilla, most holy, and of Tenedos are lord with force,
sentences.i: “Hear me, silver-bowed one, you who stand guard over Chryse and most holy Cilla, and powerfully rule Tenedos:
sentences.n: These two lines are Chryses’ opening at 37–38 word for word, and the English is the same as there. κλῦθί μευ is ‘hear me’ (μευ the epic genitive of ἐγώ), ἀργυρότοξε ‘silver-bowed one’ the vocative of Apollo’s epithet, and ὃς … ἀμφιβέβηκας ‘you who stand over’ is a perfect of ἀμφιβαίνω. Χρύσην, Κίλλαν and Τενέδοιο are places sacred to him; ζαθέην ‘most holy’ is the epithet of Cilla, and ἶφι ἀνάσσεις is ‘you are lord with force’, ‘powerfully rule’.

sentences.t:
ἦ μὲν δή ποτ’ ἐμεῦ πάρος ἔκλυες εὐξαμένοιο,
τίμησας μὲν ἐμέ, μέγα δ’ ἴψαο λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.l:
Truly indeed once before you heard me when I prayed,
you honoured me, and greatly struck the people of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: Truly, once before you heard me when I prayed: you honoured me and struck the people of the Achaeans hard;
sentences.n: Chryses reminds Apollo of the first prayer and what came of it, the plague. ἦ μὲν δή is a strong ‘truly indeed’. ἔκλυες takes the genitive, and ἐμεῦ … εὐξαμένοιο is ‘me having prayed’, with ἐμεῦ the epic form of ἐμοῦ. τίμησας μὲν ἐμέ is ‘you honoured me’ (τιμάω, the word for the honour the quarrel is about), set against μέγα δ’ ἴψαο ‘and struck hard’. ἴψαο is the aorist middle of ἴπτω, a rare verb; ‘strike hard’ is the traditional sense, and the Greek does not name the plague.

sentences.t: ἠδ’ ἔτι καὶ νῦν μοι τόδ’ ἐπικρήηνον ἐέλδωρ·
sentences.l: and still, even now, for me this fulfil, the wish;
sentences.i: and further, even now, fulfil this wish for me;
sentences.n: ἠδ’ ἔτι καὶ νῦν is ‘and further, even now’, which joins the new request to the old. ἐπικρήηνον is the aorist imperative of ἐπικραιαίνω ‘bring to pass, fulfil’, the same verb as κρήηνον at 41 with a preverb added; Thetis uses κρήηνον again at 504. τόδε … ἐέλδωρ is ‘this wish’, and the wish itself comes in the next line. The stop at the end of the line separates the request from its content.

sentences.t: ἤδη νῦν Δαναοῖσιν ἀεικέα λοιγὸν ἄμυνον.
sentences.l: even now from the Danaans unseemly ruin ward off.”
sentences.i: ward off unseemly ruin from the Danaans, even now.”
sentences.n: The request itself: that Apollo turn the plague away from the Danaans. ἄμυνον is the aorist imperative of ἀμύνω ‘ward off’, which takes the dative Δαναοῖσιν ‘from the Danaans’ (the people kept from harm) and the accusative λοιγόν ‘ruin’. ἀεικέα ‘unseemly’ and λοιγόν are the pair used at 341, where Achilles speaks of warding ruin off from the others, and at 398, where he says Thetis once warded it off from Zeus. ἤδη νῦν is ‘even now’, ‘by this time’. The prayer ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος, τοῦ δ’ ἔκλυε Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων.
sentences.l: So he spoke, praying, and him heard Phoebus Apollo.
sentences.i: So he prayed, and Phoebus Apollo heard him.
sentences.n: This is the formula that closes a prayer, and it also closed Chryses’ first, at 43. τοῦ is ‘him’ in the genitive, since κλύω ‘hear’ takes the genitive of the person heard, and ἔκλυε is the aorist of κλύω. ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος is ‘so he spoke, praying’ (ἔφατ’ is ἔφατο). The line gives no more than that the god heard; what Apollo does about it is not said in these words.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ εὔξαντο καὶ οὐλοχύτας προβάλοντο,
αὐέρυσαν μὲν πρῶτα καὶ ἔσφαξαν καὶ ἔδειραν,
μηρούς τ’ ἐξέταμον κατά τε κνίσῃ ἐκάλυψαν
δίπτυχα ποιήσαντες, ἐπ’ αὐτῶν δ’ ὠμοθέτησαν·
sentences.l:
But when they had prayed and had thrown forward the barley-for-sprinkling,
they drew back first, and slaughtered, and flayed,
the thighs they cut out and covered them over with fat,
making it double-folded, and on them they laid raw pieces;
sentences.i: When they had prayed and thrown down the barley for sprinkling, they first drew the victims’ heads back, slaughtered and flayed them, cut out the thighs, covered them with fat folded double, and laid raw morsels on them;
sentences.n: The sacrifice goes through its usual stages; lines 458, 460 and 461 are nearly the Odyssey’s, and their English is kept. αὐέρυσαν ‘drew back’ has no object in the Greek: the heads of the victims are what is understood, since the throat is cut after the head is pulled back, and the English supplies them. ἔσφαξαν is ‘slaughtered’ and ἔδειραν ‘flayed’. The thighs (μηρούς) are wrapped in κνίσῃ, which here is the fat (the dative of what covers them), not the ‘savour’ that rose to heaven at 317. δίπτυχα is ‘folded double’, and ὠμοθέτησαν ‘laid raw pieces’ on top of the thighs.

sentences.t:
καῖε δ’ ἐπὶ σχίζῃς ὁ γέρων, ἐπὶ δ’ αἴθοπα οἶνον
λεῖβε·
sentences.l:
And he burned them on split wood, the old man, and over them the fire-faced wine
poured;
sentences.i: The old man burned them on split wood and poured the wine that has the look of fire over them;
sentences.n: ὁ γέρων is ‘the old man’, Chryses, who is the priest and so does the burning. καῖε and λεῖβε are unaugmented imperfects of καίω ‘burn’ and λείβω ‘pour’, and ἐπὶ … λεῖβε has its preverb apart from the verb (tmesis), ‘poured over’. σχίζῃς is the dative plural of σχίζα ‘split wood’. αἴθοπα ‘fire-faced’ (the Odyssey’s epithet of wine) is translated every time. The line is Odyssey 3.459, and its English is kept.

sentences.t: νέοι δὲ παρ’ αὐτὸν ἔχον πεμπώβολα χερσίν.
sentences.l: and young men beside him held five-pronged forks in their hands.
sentences.i: and beside him young men held five-pronged forks in their hands.
sentences.n: νέοι is ‘young men’, the helpers at the rite. ἔχον is an unaugmented imperfect of ἔχω ‘hold’. πεμπώβολα are five-pronged forks, from Aeolic πέμπε ‘five’ (Attic πέντε) and ὀβελός ‘spit’; the line does not say what they were used for. χερσίν is a dative plural of χείρ ‘hand’. παρ’ αὐτόν, with the accusative, is ‘beside him’. The line is the Odyssey’s, and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κατὰ μῆρε κάη καὶ σπλάγχνα πάσαντο,
μίστυλλόν τ’ ἄρα τἆλλα καὶ ἀμφ’ ὀβελοῖσιν ἔπειραν,
ὤπτησάν τε περιφραδέως, ἐρύσαντό τε πάντα.
sentences.l:
But when the thigh-pieces were burned up and they had tasted the entrails,
they cut up the rest then into pieces and pierced them around spits,
and roasted them very carefully and drew them all off.
sentences.i: When the thigh-pieces were burned up and they had tasted the entrails, they cut up the rest into small pieces, pierced them on spits, roasted them with great care, and drew them all off.
sentences.n: The offering to the god is burned first and the meal is then made from the rest. μῆρε, as the edition prints it, looks like a dual (‘the pair of thighs’) where the Odyssey’s line has the plural μῆρ’; the sense is the same and the English follows the Odyssey. κάη is the aorist passive of καίω without the augment (= ἐκάη), with its preverb apart in κατὰ … κάη (tmesis), ‘was burned up’; σπλάγχνα πάσαντο is ‘they tasted the entrails’ (πάσαντο, aorist of πατέομαι). μίστυλλον and ἔπειραν are ‘cut into pieces’ and ‘pierced’, with ἀμφ’ ὀβελοῖσιν ‘around spits’; ἐρύσαντο is ‘drew off’ the roasted meat, and περιφραδέως ‘with great care’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ παύσαντο πόνου τετύκοντό τε δαῖτα
δαίνυντ’, οὐδέ τι θυμὸς ἐδεύετο δαιτὸς ἐΐσης.
sentences.l:
And when they had ceased from toil and had made ready the feast,
they feasted, and not at all did the heart lack the equal feast.
sentences.i: And when they had ended their labour and prepared the meal, they feasted, and their hearts went short of nothing in the equally shared feast.
sentences.n: The meal itself. There is no connecting word between the two halves: the ἐπεί clause ends and the main verb δαίνυντ’ (= δαίνυντο, ‘they feasted’, an unaugmented imperfect) follows at once. παύσαντο πόνου is ‘ceased from toil’, with the genitive, and τετύκοντο is a reduplicated aorist of τεύχω ‘make ready’. ἐδεύετο ‘lacked’ takes the genitive δαιτὸς ἐΐσης ‘the equal feast’, ‘equally shared’; θυμός ‘heart’ is here the seat of appetite. The line is nearly the Odyssey’s, and the English follows it.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
κοῦροι μὲν κρητῆρας ἐπεστέψαντο ποτοῖο,
νώμησαν δ’ ἄρα πᾶσιν ἐπαρξάμενοι δεπάεσσιν·
sentences.l:
But when of drink and of food they had put away desire,
young men filled the mixing-bowls to the brim with drink,
and they dealt it out to all, having first poured drops into the cups.
sentences.i: When they had put from them the desire for drink and food, young men filled the mixing-bowls to the brim with drink and served it out to all, first pouring a few drops into each cup.
sentences.n: After the meal comes the drinking. αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο is a line the two poems share: ἕντο is the aorist middle of ἵημι, ἐξ … ἕντο ‘put out from themselves’, and the genitives are ‘of drink and food’, so they ‘put away desire’. ἐπεστέψαντο ‘filled to the brim’ has the root of στέφω ‘crown’. νώμησαν is ‘dealt out’, and ἐπαρξάμενοι ‘having first poured drops’ (ἐπάρχομαι) goes with δεπάεσσιν ‘into the cups’, the dative plural of δέπας. The English follows the Odyssey’s for the same words.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ πανημέριοι μολπῇ θεὸν ἱλάσκοντο
καλὸν ἀείδοντες παιήονα κοῦροι Ἀχαιῶν
μέλποντες ἑκάεργον·
sentences.i: And all day long the young men of the Achaeans appeased the god with song and dance, singing a fair paean and celebrating the god who works from afar;
sentences.n: Their hymn to the god they are trying to please. οἳ δέ are the crew; πανημέριοι is ‘all day long’, ἱλάσκοντο ‘were appeasing’, and μολπῇ ‘with song and dance’. παιήονα is a paean, a song addressed to Apollo; καλόν is ‘fair’. μέλποντες, ‘celebrating’, is from the same root as μολπή and means singing and dancing in honour of someone. ἑκάεργον is ‘far-working’, with the epithet’s meaning disputed (‘far-working’ or ‘far-shooting’), and here it names the god once more as the one being praised.

sentences.t: ὃ δὲ φρένα τέρπετ’ ἀκούων.
sentences.l: and he in mind took delight, hearing.
sentences.i: and in his mind he took delight as he listened.
sentences.n: ὃ δέ is ‘and he’ (the article as a pronoun), Apollo, who is shown pleased by the hymn. φρένα is an accusative of respect, ‘in his mind’, and τέρπετ’ is τέρπετο ‘took delight’, an imperfect. ἀκούων is ‘hearing’. This half-line is one of the places where the edition ends a sentence in the middle of a verse.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠέλιος κατέδυ καὶ ἐπὶ κνέφας ἦλθε,
δὴ τότε κοιμήσαντο παρὰ πρυμνήσια νηός·
sentences.l:
And when the sun set and darkness came on,
then indeed they lay down to sleep beside the stern-cables of the ship;
sentences.i: And when the sun set and darkness came on, then they lay down to sleep beside the ship’s stern-cables;
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and a night passes. The first line is the sunset formula the Odyssey uses, with its English kept: ἠέλιος is the epic form of ἥλιος ‘sun’, κνέφας is ‘darkness’, and ἐπὶ … ἦλθε ‘came on’ has the preverb apart from the verb (tmesis). κοιμήσαντο is the aorist middle of κοιμάω, ‘put themselves to sleep’, ‘lay down to sleep’. παρὰ πρυμνήσια are ‘beside the stern-cables’, the ones made fast ashore at 436.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
καὶ τότ’ ἔπειτ’ ἀνάγοντο μετὰ στρατὸν εὐρὺν Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.l:
When early-born appeared, rose-fingered Dawn,
then thereupon they put out to sea toward the wide army of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, then they put out to sea for the wide army of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: The dawn formula of the Odyssey, with its English kept: ἠριγένεια ‘early-born’ and ῥοδοδάκτυλος ‘rose-fingered’ are the stock epithets of Ἠώς ‘Dawn’, translated every time. ἀνάγοντο is the imperfect middle of ἀνάγω, ‘put out to sea’ (literally ‘led themselves up’), and μετὰ στρατόν, with the accusative, is ‘toward the army’. εὐρύς ‘wide’ is the epithet of the army here and at 484.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ ἴκμενον οὖρον ἵει ἑκάεργος Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.l: and for them a favouring wind sent far-working Apollo;
sentences.i: and Apollo, who works from afar, sent them a favouring wind;
sentences.n: The god they have just appeased sends them home. ἵει is the imperfect of ἵημι ‘send’. ἴκμενον οὖρον is ‘a favouring wind’: the sense of ἴκμενος is not certain, and ‘favouring’ is the traditional gloss, as in the Odyssey. ἑκάεργος ‘far-working’ is Apollo’s epithet, translated here as in the Odyssey; its meaning is disputed (‘far-working’ or ‘far-shooting’).

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἱστὸν στήσαντ’ ἀνά θ’ ἱστία λευκὰ πέτασσαν,
ἐν δ’ ἄνεμος πρῆσεν μέσον ἱστίον, ἀμφὶ δὲ κῦμα
στείρῃ πορφύρεον μεγάλ’ ἴαχε νηὸς ἰούσης·
sentences.i: They set up the mast and spread the white sails, and the wind filled the belly of the sail, and the surging wave roared loudly about the stem as the ship went on her way;
sentences.n: Under sail. ἱστὸν στήσαντο is ‘set up the mast’, and ἀνά … πέτασσαν ‘spread out’ has its preverb apart from the verb, with ἱστία λευκά ‘white sails’. ἐν … πρῆσεν is ‘blew into, filled’, again in tmesis, with μέσον ἱστίον ‘the middle of the sail’ as object; ‘belly’ is the usual name for that part. Lines 481–482 are also Odyssey 2.427–428, except that there the verb stands first and whole (ἔπρησεν δ’ ἄνεμος) where here it is split (ἐν δ’ ἄνεμος πρῆσεν), and the English is kept. στείρῃ is ‘at the stem’; πορφύρεον ‘surging’ is a word with a colour sense, ‘dark, purple’, here used of the heaving wave; ἴαχε is ‘resounded’, and νηὸς ἰούσης is a genitive absolute, ‘the ship going’.

sentences.t: ἣ δ’ ἔθεεν κατὰ κῦμα διαπρήσσουσα κέλευθον.
sentences.l: and she ran over the wave, accomplishing the way.
sentences.i: and she ran over the wave, completing her way.
sentences.n: ἣ is the ship, feminine and so ‘she’. ἔθεεν is the imperfect of θέω ‘run’, a verb Homer often uses of a ship under sail. κατὰ κῦμα is ‘over the wave’, and διαπρήσσουσα ‘accomplishing’ (διαπρήσσω, ‘get through, accomplish’) goes with κέλευθον ‘way’, as in the Odyssey’s ‘accomplish the way’; the preverb διά- suggests going through to the end.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἵκοντο κατὰ στρατὸν εὐρὺν Ἀχαιῶν,
νῆα μὲν οἵ γε μέλαιναν ἐπ’ ἠπείροιο ἔρυσσαν
ὑψοῦ ἐπὶ ψαμάθοις, ὑπὸ δ’ ἕρματα μακρὰ τάνυσσαν·
sentences.i: When they reached the wide army of the Achaeans, they drew the black ship up onto the dry land, high up on the sands, and stretched long props beneath it;
sentences.n: The ship is beached for a long stay. κατὰ στρατόν, with the accusative, is ‘among the army’; the second line is the Odyssey’s, with its English kept, though there ἤπειρος is ‘dry land’ against ‘mainland’ elsewhere. ἔρυσσαν is ‘drew’ (ἐρύω), ὑψοῦ ‘high up’, ψαμάθοις ‘on the sands’ (a dative plural), and ὑπὸ … τάνυσσαν ‘stretched beneath’ has the preverb apart from the verb. ἕρματα here are props, supports that hold the hull off the ground.

sentences.t: αὐτοὶ δ’ ἐσκίδναντο κατὰ κλισίας τε νέας τε.
sentences.l: and they themselves scattered among the huts and the ships.
sentences.i: and they themselves scattered among the huts and the ships.
sentences.n: νέας here is the short accusative plural of ναῦς ‘ship’ (the Attic accusative is ναῦς, Homer’s usual is νῆας), not the adjective νέος ‘new’. αὐτοί ‘they themselves’ sets the men against the ship they have just beached. ἐσκίδναντο is an imperfect middle of σκίδνημι ‘scatter’, and κλισίας are the huts of the camp, the word used of Achilles’ own hut at 322.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ μήνιε νηυσὶ παρήμενος ὠκυπόροισι
διογενὴς Πηλῆος υἱὸς πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.l:
But he was wrathful, by the swift-faring ships sitting,
Zeus-sprung son of Peleus, swift-in-feet Achilles;
sentences.i: But he, Achilles, swift of foot, the Zeus-born son of Peleus, sat in wrath beside his swift-faring ships;
sentences.n: The camp returns to Achilles, and his name comes last, after the participle and two epithets. ὃ is ‘he’, and μήνιε ‘was wrathful’ is the verb of μῆνις, the wrath of the poem’s first word. παρήμενος ‘sitting beside’ repeats the word of Thetis’ command at 421. διογενής ‘Zeus-sprung’ and πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift in feet’ are stock epithets, translated even though he sits still; Πηλῆος is the genitive of Πηλεύς with the epic ending -ῆος.

sentences.t:
οὔτέ ποτ’ εἰς ἀγορὴν πωλέσκετο κυδιάνειραν
οὔτέ ποτ’ ἐς πόλεμον, ἀλλὰ φθινύθεσκε φίλον κῆρ
αὖθι μένων, ποθέεσκε δ’ ἀϋτήν τε πτόλεμόν τε.
sentences.l:
Neither ever to the man-glorifying assembly did he go,
nor ever to war, but he kept wasting his dear heart
staying there on the spot, and he kept longing for the battle-cry and for war.
sentences.i: He never went to the assembly that brings men glory, nor ever to war, but kept wasting away his dear heart as he stayed there, and longed for the battle-cry and for war.
sentences.n: What Achilles does while he sits: nothing, and the verbs say it is a habit, not a single act. πωλέσκετο, φθινύθεσκε and ποθέεσκε carry the iterative suffix -σκ-, ‘used to go’, ‘kept wasting’, ‘kept longing’. ἀγορή is the assembly, and its epithet κυδιάνειρα ‘man-glorifying’ (κῦδος ‘glory’ + ἀνήρ ‘man’) says it is a place where men win glory. φθινύθω is ‘waste away’, with φίλον κῆρ ‘his dear heart’ as object; αὖθι is ‘there, on the spot’, and ἀϋτή is ‘battle-cry’. πτόλεμον is the epic form of πόλεμον ‘war’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἐκ τοῖο δυωδεκάτη γένετ’ ἠώς,
καὶ τότε δὴ πρὸς Ὄλυμπον ἴσαν θεοὶ αἰὲν ἐόντες
πάντες ἅμα, Ζεὺς δ’ ἦρχε·
sentences.i: But when the twelfth dawn had come after that day, the gods who are forever went to Olympus all together, and Zeus led the way;
sentences.n: The twelve days that Thetis named at 425 are counted out. ἐκ τοῖο is ‘from that (day)’, leaving the day unnamed. δυωδεκάτη is the Homeric form of δωδεκάτη ‘twelfth’, and ἠώς ‘dawn’ is feminine, so it is the twelfth dawn. γένετ’ is an unaugmented aorist, ‘came to be’. θεοὶ αἰὲν ἐόντες, ‘the gods who are forever’, is the formula for the undying gods. ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’ in the plural, and ἦρχε ‘led the way’ is Zeus’s part: he goes first, as he went first to the feast.

sentences.t:
Θέτις δ’ οὐ λήθετ’ ἐφετμέων
παιδὸς ἑοῦ, ἀλλ’ ἥ γ’ ἀνεδύσετο κῦμα θαλάσσης.
sentences.l:
and Thetis did not forget the commands
of her own child, but she rose up out of the wave of the sea.
sentences.i: and Thetis did not forget her child’s commands, but rose up out of the wave of the sea.
sentences.n: Thetis keeps her promise. λήθετ’ is an unaugmented imperfect of λήθομαι ‘forget’ and takes the genitive ἐφετμέων ‘commands’, here the requests Achilles made to her at 352–412. ἑοῦ is the possessive ‘her own’ (the possessive ὅς, not the relative), and ἥ γ’ is ‘she’, the article as a pronoun with γε, ‘she for her part’. ἀνεδύσετο is the same kind of aorist as ἀπεβήσετο at 428, ‘rose up’, here with the accusative κῦμα θαλάσσης ‘out of the wave of the sea’.

sentences.t: ἠερίη δ’ ἀνέβη μέγαν οὐρανὸν Οὔλυμπόν τε.
sentences.l: and morning-early she went up to great heaven and Olympus.
sentences.i: and early in the morning she went up to great heaven and to Olympus.
sentences.n: ἠερίη is a word whose meaning is not certain: ‘early in the morning’ is the usual explanation and the one used here, while others connect it with ἀήρ ‘mist’, giving ‘in the mist’. ἀνέβη is ‘went up’. μέγαν οὐρανὸν Οὔλυμπόν τε is ‘great heaven and Olympus’: sky and mountain are named together as the goal, and the edition spells the mountain with Οὐ- here, as at 425.

sentences.t:
εὗρεν δ’ εὐρύοπα Κρονίδην ἄτερ ἥμενον ἄλλων
ἀκροτάτῃ κορυφῇ πολυδειράδος Οὐλύμποιο·
sentences.l:
and she found far-thundering the son-of-Cronus sitting apart from the others
on the topmost peak of many-ridged Olympus;
sentences.i: and she found the son of Cronus, who thunders from afar, sitting apart from the others on the topmost peak of many-ridged Olympus;
sentences.n: Zeus is alone, which is what Thetis needs. εὗρεν is ‘found’, and Κρονίδην ‘son of Cronus’ names Zeus; εὐρύοπα is his epithet, accusative, ‘far-thundering’, translated every time, though the second part of the word (from ὄψ ‘voice’ or ‘eye, face’) is disputed and ‘far-thundering’ is the traditional gloss. ἄτερ ἄλλων is ‘apart from the others’ (ἄτερ takes the genitive), and ἥμενον is ‘sitting’. ἀκροτάτῃ κορυφῇ is ‘on the topmost peak’, a dative of place, and πολυδειράδος ‘many-ridged’ (πολύ- + δειράς ‘ridge’) is the epithet of Olympus.

sentences.t:
καί ῥα πάροιθ’ αὐτοῖο καθέζετο, καὶ λάβε γούνων
σκαιῇ, δεξιτερῇ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπ’ ἀνθερεῶνος ἑλοῦσα
λισσομένη προσέειπε Δία Κρονίωνα ἄνακτα·
sentences.l:
and then she sat down before him, and took hold of his knees
with her left hand, and with her right, taking him under the chin,
begging, she addressed Zeus, the son of Cronus, the lord:
sentences.i: She sat down before him and took hold of his knees with her left hand, and with her right hand under his chin, begging, she spoke to lord Zeus, the son of Cronus:
sentences.n: The suppliant’s hold, spelled out: the knees with one hand and the chin with the other. Thetis does what Achilles told her at 407, λαβὲ γούνων ‘take hold of his knees’, here λάβε γούνων with the genitive of the part held. σκαιῇ is ‘with the left (hand)’ and δεξιτερῇ ‘with the right’; ὑπ’ ἀνθερεῶνος ἑλοῦσα is ‘taking him under the chin’. καθέζετο is ‘sat down’, πάροιθ’ αὐτοῖο ‘in front of him’, and λισσομένη ‘begging’. προσέειπε ‘addressed’ takes Δία Κρονίωνα ἄνακτα ‘Zeus, the son of Cronus, the lord’.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ εἴ ποτε δή σε μετ’ ἀθανάτοισιν ὄνησα
ἢ ἔπει ἢ ἔργῳ, τόδε μοι κρήηνον ἐέλδωρ·
sentences.l:
“Zeus father, if ever indeed among the immortals I helped you
either by a word or by a deed, this for me fulfil, the wish:
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, if ever I helped you among the immortals, whether by word or by deed, fulfil this wish for me:
sentences.n: Her plea rests on a claim of service, the argument Achilles gave her at 394–395 (whether by word or by deed). Ζεῦ πάτερ is the vocative, ‘Zeus father’. εἴ ποτε δή σε … ὄνησα is ‘if ever indeed I helped you’: ὄνησα is the aorist of ὀνίνημι ‘help, benefit’. ἔπει is the dative of ἔπος ‘word’ and ἔργῳ the dative of ἔργον ‘deed’. τόδε … κρήηνον ἐέλδωρ ‘fulfil this wish’ uses the same words as Chryses in his first prayer at 41 (at 455 with a preverb added); the wish itself is given in the next lines.

sentences.t:
τίμησόν μοι υἱὸν ὃς ὠκυμορώτατος ἄλλων
ἔπλετ’·
sentences.l:
Honour for me my son, who most swift-doomed of the others
has become;
sentences.i: Honour for me my son, who has come to be the swiftest of all to his doom;
sentences.n: The wish begins with the thing Achilles has lost, honour. τίμησον is the aorist imperative of τιμάω ‘honour’, with μοι ‘for me’ and υἱόν ‘son’. ὠκυμορώτατος is ‘most swift-doomed’, the superlative of the ὠκύμορος she used of him at 417, and ἄλλων is the genitive of comparison, ‘than the others’. ἔπλετ’ is ἔπλετο ‘has become’ (πέλομαι, like ἔπλεο at 418). The edition ends the clause in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
ἀτάρ μιν νῦν γε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων
ἠτίμησεν· ἑλὼν γὰρ ἔχει γέρας αὐτὸς ἀπούρας.
sentences.l:
but him now at least the lord of men, Agamemnon,
has dishonoured; for he has taken and holds the prize, himself having taken it away;
sentences.i: but now Agamemnon, lord of men, has dishonoured him; for he has taken his prize of honour and keeps it, having seized it himself;
sentences.n: Her complaint ends with Achilles’ own words at 356, the second line here being word for word the same, with ‘his’ for ‘my’ in the English. ἀτάρ is ‘but’, μιν is ‘him’ (Achilles), and νῦν γε ‘now at least’ marks the contrast with his short life. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν is ‘lord of men’. ἠτίμησεν is ‘has dishonoured’, and ἑλὼν … ἀπούρας, two aorist participles, are ‘having taken, having taken away’, with ἔχει ‘holds’. γέρας is the prize of honour, a share set apart for a leader. αὐτός ‘himself’ puts the act on Agamemnon, though his heralds carried it out.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ σύ πέρ μιν τῖσον Ὀλύμπιε μητίετα Ζεῦ·
sentences.l: But you at least honour him, Olympian counsellor Zeus;
sentences.i: But you, at least, honour him, Olympian Zeus the counsellor;
sentences.n: The request in its plainest form. τῖσον is the aorist imperative of τίω ‘honour’ (the verb of ἔτισεν at 412), with μιν ‘him’. The form could be read as from τίνω ‘pay’, but with τίμησον, τιμῇ and the honour at stake all around it ‘honour’ is the sense that fits. σύ πέρ is ‘you at least’, setting Zeus against Agamemnon, who has not. Ὀλύμπιε ‘Olympian’ and μητίετα ‘counsellor’ (from μῆτις ‘counsel, cunning’) are vocatives with Ζεῦ.

sentences.t:
τόφρα δ’ ἐπὶ Τρώεσσι τίθει κράτος ὄφρ’ ἂν Ἀχαιοὶ
υἱὸν ἐμὸν τίσωσιν ὀφέλλωσίν τέ ἑ τιμῇ.
sentences.l:
and meanwhile upon the Trojans put strength, until the Achaeans
my son shall honour and shall increase him with honour.”
sentences.i: and in the meantime give strength to the Trojans, until the Achaeans honour my son and increase him in honour.”
sentences.n: The second request, which will turn the war against the Achaeans until they pay him honour. τόφρα δέ is ‘and meanwhile’, answered by ὄφρ’ ἂν ‘until’ with the subjunctive. ἐπὶ Τρώεσσι τίθει κράτος is ‘put strength upon the Trojans’ (τίθει is the present imperative of τίθημι); κράτος is strength and may mean the upper hand, but the Greek says only strength. τίσωσιν ‘shall honour’ is the verb of 508, and ὀφέλλωσιν ‘shall increase’ comes from ὀφέλλω ‘increase’, a different verb from the ὄφελες ‘ought’ of 415; ἑ is ‘him’ and τιμῇ ‘with honour’. Her speech ends here, inside this part.
